domain: Cold email outreach (UK, B2B), sent through the customer's own Microsoft 365 / Google Workspace mailbox
summary: Outreach is sent via Microsoft Graph POST /users/{mailbox}/sendMail or the Gmail API, through the customer's OWN tenant, from their own address, into their own Sent Items. Sending through ODoutreach IS sending from Outlook. This single fact changes the domain requirements materially: there is no second sending domain, so SPF already aligns and DMARC passes on SPF alignment alone. The customer needs ZERO DNS changes. The unavoidable ask is Entra admin consent - identity, not DNS.
supersession_note: Section 6 of the prose brief (30 July) recommends building a Sending Domain Readiness Gate that verifies SPF/DKIM/DMARC by live DNS lookup before allowing a send. That recommendation was written BEFORE the 6 August transport finding and is largely moot for the Graph/Gmail path, where authentication is inherited from the customer's existing corporate mail setup. It remains valid for any send that does NOT go through a connected mailbox. The prose brief has not been edited; this field records the supersession so the stale recommendation is not implemented by mistake.

email_authentication.note: SPF/DKIM/DMARC and alignment. Researched 2026-07-30 from cited sources, then verified 2026-08-06 against the actual transport. Key fact: DMARC passes if EITHER SPF or DKIM aligns; Graph sending aligns SPF, so DMARC passes with or without a published DMARC record. Exchange signs as <tenant>.onmicrosoft.com without custom DKIM, so DKIM alignment fails - this is not fatal. Custom DKIM and DMARC make it better, not possible.

link_alignment_and_phishing_heuristics.note: The ACTUAL root cause of the 2026 quarantine incident. Unsubscribe links and the open-tracking pixel pointed at the ODoutreach app domain while From: was the customer's domain - the textbook phishing pattern. This causes per-message quarantine; sustained quarantine plus complaints then degrades reputation, which is why it presented as domain damage. Note the ambiguity that caused confusion: 'domain mismatch' means DMARC alignment in the protocol sense, and links-not-matching-sender in the everyday sense. Only the first is an authentication failure.

volume_warmup_and_throttling.note: Industry norm is 4-6 mailboxes per sending domain at 40-50/day each. ODoutreach enforces 5 mailboxes at 30/day - MORE conservative than the standard, and correct. The volume logic was never the problem. A 30-day warm-up from zero is required for a new mailbox or domain.

uk_pecr_and_gdpr.note: PECR Regulation 22 plus UK GDPR. The distinction that matters is the recipient's LEGAL STRUCTURE, not whether they are 'a business': corporate subscribers (limited companies, LLPs, public bodies) need no prior consent; individual subscribers (sole traders, unincorporated partnerships, personal addresses) do. A one-person limited company falls under the carve-out; a sole trader does not. NOT LEGAL ADVICE - the prose brief says to confirm with a solicitor before relying on this commercially, and that confirmation has NOT been obtained. Recorded as an open item in SCOPE.md section 6.

deliverability_thresholds.note: Complaint rate below 0.1% and never reaching 0.3%; bounce rate below 2% overall (Gmail reputation review at 2%, Microsoft 365 throttles at 1.5%, Yahoo tolerates ~2.5%). KNOWLEDGE is Working. Automated enforcement is NOT built - bounce/complaint auto-halt is Phase 4 and explicitly out of scope for August. Hard-bounce suppression IS live and enabled.

domain_reputation_recovery.note: Diagnose via Google Postmaster Tools and blacklist checks, stop sending, re-warm from zero over 4-6 weeks, reintroduce cautiously. Retire rather than recover if on multiple major blacklists with delisting refused, or if 6-8 weeks of clean warm-up shows no improvement. Standing up a fresh correctly-configured domain takes 3-4 weeks. Does not gate a send in this product because the customer's own mailbox is the transport.

non_negotiables.requirement: Every sending domain must have SPF, DKIM and DMARC, and the From: domain must align with SPF or DKIM. DMARC passes if EITHER aligns.
non_negotiables.applies_here: Satisfied inherently by the Graph/Gmail transport - the customer's existing SPF already authorises Microsoft's or Google's IPs, or they could not send mail at all today.

non_negotiables.requirement: Bulk senders (5,000+/day to one provider) are subject to the full bulk-sender rules. Enforced by Google and Yahoo since 2024 and by Microsoft since 5 May 2025; Gmail escalated to permanent rejections in November 2025.
non_negotiables.applies_here: Not currently reached - 5 mailboxes at 30/day is 150/day per workspace.

non_negotiables.requirement: Spam complaint rate must stay below 0.10% and must NEVER reach 0.30%. There is NO published bounce-rate threshold from any provider — see note.
non_negotiables.source: https://support.google.com/a/answer/81126 — Google's own Email sender guidelines, fetched 2026-08-23. Verbatim: "Keep spam rates reported in Postmaster Tools below 0.10% and avoid ever reaching a spam rate of 0.30% or higher."
non_negotiables.applies_here: Complaint capture is live (MAILBOX_COMPLAINT_DETECTION_ENABLED=true in production). Automated auto-halt on a rising rate is NOT built — no send path reads the rate, so a person has to notice.
non_negotiables.correction_2026_08_23: The previous version of this non-negotiable asserted 'bounce rate must stay below 2%' sourced to redsift.com, a vendor guide. Google's own sender guidelines were fetched on 2026-08-23 and publish NO bounce-rate or error-rate threshold. The 2% figure is a widely-repeated industry heuristic with no provider backing. It has been REMOVED as a provider requirement. What Google actually publishes is a BEHAVIOURAL rule, recorded separately below. Keeping 2% as an internal operating target is fine; presenting it as a provider threshold was not.

non_negotiables.requirement: A functional opt-out must be present and honoured, and opt-outs processed within 2 days. List-Unsubscribe must be present and functional.
non_negotiables.applies_here: Satisfied by the mailto: rail plus a visible plain-English opt-out line; reply ingestion auto-suppresses via classifyOptOutReply. Gated in code - see irreversible_actions.

non_negotiables.requirement: An outreach email may be sent from the client's own primary business mailbox. What must hold instead — all four, together — is: (1) every link in the email is on a domain ALIGNED with the From: domain, or there is no link at all; (2) SPF, DKIM and DMARC pass on the sending domain; (3) sending volume ramps on SENDING HISTORY, per Google's published guidance; (4) the spam-complaint rate stays below 0.10% and never reaches 0.30%.
non_negotiables.source: Greg's ruling 2026-08-24 (quoted below) for the architectural choice; the four replacement protections are each independently sourced — link alignment from the 2026 incident root cause and https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/blog/microsoftdefenderforoffice365blog/strengthening-email-ecosystem-outlook%E2%80%99s-new-requirements-for-high%E2%80%90volume-senders/4399730 ('From/Reply-To must reflect the true sending domain'); volume ramp and complaint thresholds from https://support.google.com/a/answer/81126, fetched 2026-08-23.
non_negotiables.rewritten_because: The rule was wrong, not the product. A separate sending domain is the right shape for high-volume cold-email INFRASTRUCTURE, where domains are consumable and a burnt one is replaced. This product is deliberately not that: it sends from the client's own mailbox, as the client, at roughly 1.5% of the provider's per-mailbox ceiling, with a real human reply-to. That is closer to a salesperson sending by hand than to a bulk sender, and it is the thing that makes the product distinctive. The old rule also BLAMED THE WRONG CAUSE: the 2026 quarantine was not caused by sending from the client's domain. It was caused by the LINK domain not matching the From: domain — the phishing pattern — which is now fixed, tested and live.
non_negotiables.greg_ruling_verbatim: RULING 2, 2026-08-24: 'the sending-domain non-negotiable is WRONG. Rewrite it.' — 'the rule is wrong, not the product.'

how_each_replacement_is_enforced.1_link_alignment: ENFORCED AND TESTED. resolveUnsubscribeRail (src/lib/unsubscribe/one-click-readiness.ts) mints a hosted link ONLY from a base URL the caller has confirmed is sender-aligned, and falls to a mailto: rail on the sending mailbox otherwise. send-introduction.ts does not import resolvePublicBaseUrl at all, so the app domain cannot leak back in by accident. Tests: one-click-readiness.test.ts 'does NOT read the app base URL from the environment', 'falls to mailto when there is no aligned domain — the normal case today', 'returns none when neither rail is available'; send-introduction.test.ts 'BLOCKS a non-allowlisted real-prospect send when NO opt-out rail exists at all'. Plus scripts/ops-cross-domain-audit.ts as a site-wide sweep.
how_each_replacement_is_enforced.2_spf_dkim_dmarc: SATISFIED INHERENTLY by the transport. Sending through the client's own Microsoft 365 / Google Workspace mailbox means the provider signs the mail on the client's own domain — their existing SPF already authorises those IPs, or they could not send ordinary business mail today. This is the whole reason the zero-DNS model works.
how_each_replacement_is_enforced.3_ramp_on_sending_history: NOT SATISFIED AS AT 2026-08-24. mailbox-warmup.ts ramps on mailbox AGE (connectedAt), not sends made. Its own docstring concedes any mailbox older than the ramp window is unaffected, so a long-connected but never-used mailbox starts at full allowance. Being fixed under BUILD-2 item 1.
how_each_replacement_is_enforced.4_complaint_rate: MEASURED BUT NOT ACTED ON. MAILBOX_COMPLAINT_DETECTION_ENABLED is true in production, so complaints are captured and suppress the address. No send path reads the RATE, so nothing throttles when it climbs. See the volume-response non-negotiable.

accepted_residual_risk.risk: Because outreach goes out on the client's PRIMARY business domain, there is NO FALLBACK if that domain's reputation is damaged. The same domain carries their invoices, contracts and ordinary customer mail. A disposable sending subdomain would absorb that damage; there isn't one. Recovery, per the domain brief, is 4-6 weeks of re-warming with no outreach at all — during which their normal business email is also degraded.
accepted_residual_risk.in_exchange_for: Requiring no DNS changes from the client, which is the product's distinctive onboarding advantage and the reason clients say yes.
accepted_residual_risk.what_makes_it_tolerable: Low volume (30/day/mailbox, ~1.5% of the provider ceiling), the client's own tenant as transport, a real human reply-to, and the phishing signal that caused the 2026 incident now removed and tested.
accepted_residual_risk.what_would_make_it_intolerable: Volume rising toward bulk, or a client whose domain reputation is business-critical and who has not been told. THIS RISK MUST BE STATED TO EVERY CLIENT IN WRITING before their mailbox is connected — it is their domain being wagered, not OpensDoors'.
accepted_residual_risk.reversal_trigger: If a client's primary domain is ever degraded by outreach, the subdomain shape stops being optional. It is a ONE-WAY DOOR once mailboxes exist — moving means provisioning NEW mailboxes on mail.<client-domain> and having the client sign in to them, which is a different product shape, not a setting.

superseded_rule._note: Kept visible, not deleted. The line was in force from 2026-07-30 to 2026-08-24 and anything decided under it should be re-read against the rewrite.
superseded_rule.requirement: Never send cold email from the client's primary business domain; use a dedicated secondary domain or subdomain. A subdomain does NOT inherit the parent's SPF/DKIM/DMARC and needs its own.
superseded_rule.why_superseded: Correct for high-volume cold-email infrastructure; wrong for this product, and it attributed the 2026 quarantine to the sending domain when the actual cause was link/From misalignment. Superseded by Greg's Ruling 2, 2026-08-24. The SUBDOMAIN FACT within it remains true and worth keeping: a subdomain does NOT inherit its parent's SPF/DKIM/DMARC and would need its own records — which is exactly why adopting the subdomain shape would reintroduce the DNS burden this product exists to avoid.

non_negotiables.requirement: UK: corporate subscribers (limited companies, LLPs, public bodies) may be emailed without prior consent. Individual subscribers (sole traders, unincorporated partnerships, personal addresses) require consent or soft opt-in.
non_negotiables.applies_here: NOT ENFORCED IN CODE. The contact-import pipeline cannot distinguish a sole trader from a limited company. Flagged in the prose brief as a genuine billable feature with a compliance justification. Not yet scoped into any phase.

non_negotiables.requirement: Truthful identification is always required regardless of recipient type: real sender name, real company identity, genuine reply address, no deceptive subject lines.
non_negotiables.applies_here: Satisfied - mail comes from the customer's own named mailbox and replies return to it.

non_negotiables.requirement: When messages start bouncing or being deferred, REDUCE sending volume until the error rate drops, then increase slowly again. This is a behavioural rule, not a threshold — there is no number to be under, only a direction to move in.
non_negotiables.source: https://support.google.com/a/answer/81126 — fetched 2026-08-23. Verbatim: "If messages start bouncing or start being deferred, reduce the sending volume until the SMTP error rate decreases. Then, increase slowly again." And: "Start with a low sending volume to engaged users, and slowly increase the volume over time."
non_negotiables.applies_here: NOT IMPLEMENTED. Nothing in the send path reads the bounce or error rate, so nothing can reduce volume in response to it. The 20/day ceiling is a static compensating control standing in for this rule, and it is static precisely because the rate cannot currently be read.
non_negotiables.implementation_status: DEFERRED, with a trigger — recorded 2026-08-24 rather than left stated-and-unimplemented.

deferral.reason: A rate-responsive throttle cannot be built on a rate that cannot be read. The bounce figure is structurally stuck at 0% because the NDR path never sets OutboundEmail.status=BOUNCED (see diagnoses/BOUNCE-0PCT), and that status is what every metric counts. Building an automatic volume reducer on top of that today would produce a control that never fires and looks like protection — worse than no control, because it would be believed.
deferral.trigger: BOTH: (1) the bounce status write lands so the rate is readable, and (2) at least 200 sends have been measured through it so the rate means something. Then build the reducer.
deferral.compensating_control_until_then: The static daily ceiling, which does not need to read anything. It is the substitute for a control that can respond, and it is why the ceiling may not be raised on the strength of a good deploy.

non_negotiables.requirement: Per-mailbox provider ceilings, Google Workspace: 2,000 messages per user per day; 3,000 total external recipients per day; 2,000 UNIQUE EXTERNAL recipients per day. Applied over a rolling 24-hour window, not a calendar day.
non_negotiables.applies_here: NOT the binding constraint. The product caps a mailbox at 30/day, roughly 1.5% of the unique-external-recipient ceiling. Reputation, not provider quota, is what limits this system.

non_negotiables.requirement: Per-mailbox provider ceilings, Microsoft 365 / Exchange Online: Recipient rate limit 10,000 recipients per day per mailbox; Message rate limit 30 messages per MINUTE per mailbox; recipient limit customisable up to 1,000 per message. Plus a TENANT-wide Tenant External Recipient Rate Limit (TERRL) scaled to licence count, visible in EAC Reports > Mail flow. Mail from default onmicrosoft.com domains is throttled to 100 external recipients per organisation per 24h.
non_negotiables.applies_here: Per-mailbox limits are not binding at 30/day. TERRL IS worth knowing because it is TENANT-wide, not per-mailbox: a client running several outreach mailboxes in one tenant shares one external-recipient budget. Nobody has checked any client's TERRL. Microsoft's own footnote states plainly that 'Exchange Online isn't suited to accommodate bulk-mailing scenarios' and points high-volume senders at Azure Communication Services — worth recording as the vendor's own view of this architecture, even though 150/day/client is nowhere near bulk.

non_negotiables.requirement: High-volume sender rules bite at 5,000+ messages per day to Microsoft consumer services from one From: domain: SPF and DKIM must both pass, DMARC must be published, and at least one of SPF/DKIM must ALIGN with the 5322.From domain. Since 5 May 2025 non-compliant mail is rejected outright with '550 5.7.515 Access denied, sending domain does not meet the required authentication level'. Microsoft's stated best practice alongside it: From/Reply-To must reflect the true sending domain, a functional unsubscribe must be present, and invalid addresses removed regularly.
non_negotiables.applies_here: The 5,000/day threshold is not reached. The ALIGNMENT principle applies regardless of volume and is exactly what the 2026 quarantine was about — Microsoft naming 'From/Reply-To must reflect the true sending domain' independently corroborates the zero-DNS fix shipped on 2026-08-23.

non_negotiables.requirement: WARM-UP MUST BE DRIVEN BY SENDING HISTORY, NOT BY HOW LONG A MAILBOX HAS EXISTED.
non_negotiables.source: https://support.google.com/a/answer/81126 — fetched 2026-08-23. Verbatim: "Avoid introducing sudden volume spikes if you do not have a history of sending large volumes." The condition Google states is a history of SENDING, not an account age.
non_negotiables.applies_here: **NOT SATISFIED — this is the finding.** src/lib/mailboxes/mailbox-warmup.ts anchors the ramp to mailboxAgeDays(), computed from connectedAt (else createdAt). Its own docstring says: 'any mailbox already older than the ramp window is unaffected — its effective cap is its configured cap.' So a mailbox connected three months ago that has NEVER SENT gets its full 30/day on its very first send, with no ramp at all. That is precisely the case being created now: mailboxes connected during onboarding but not yet launched. The ramp's SHAPE is fine and is more conservative than the researched schedule; its ANCHOR measures the wrong thing.

irreversible_actions.action: Dispatch an outreach email to a real prospect through a connected mailbox
irreversible_actions.gate: src/server/email/outbound/execute-one.ts - executeOutboundSend routes any row with a mailboxIdentityId to sendViaConnectedMailboxOrFail, which has NO ESP fallback: if the connected mailbox cannot send, the row fails rather than silently rerouting. Layered with evaluateSuppression (suppression-guard.ts), the client send-governance decision, and the per-mailbox daily cap in sending-policy.ts.
irreversible_actions.evidence: src/server/outreach/suppression-guard.test.ts returns skipped_missing_email on null/empty/undefined rather than proceeding; src/lib/clients/client-send-governance.test.ts asserts 'blocks a non-allowlisted recipient even if client is LIVE_PROSPECT-approved' and 'blocks non-allowlisted recipients when client is ONBOARDING'; src/server/mailbox/sending-policy.test.ts asserts errorCode MAILBOX_DAILY_CAP. All verified passing 2026-08-09.

irreversible_actions.action: Send an outreach email that carries no working opt-out, or whose links point at a domain that does not match the sender (the 2026 quarantine root cause)
irreversible_actions.gate: src/lib/unsubscribe/one-click-readiness.ts resolves the opt-out rail as hosted-on-the-client's-aligned-domain OR mailto, and returns none when neither is available. Commit a8d777c removed the app-domain fallback entirely and stopped importing resolvePublicBaseUrl into that module so it cannot return by accident.
irreversible_actions.evidence: src/lib/unsubscribe/one-click-readiness.test.ts asserts 'returns none when neither rail is available', 'returns none when the sending address is not a usable opt-out target', and the regression test 'does NOT read the app base URL from the environment'. Verified passing 2026-08-09.

irreversible_actions.action: Mark an outreach email as SENT when no mail actually left the system
irreversible_actions.gate: src/server/email/outbound/prospect-send-transport-guard.ts - evaluateProspectSendTransport() refuses any row that carries a contactId (i.e. is addressed to a real prospect) but has no mailboxIdentityId. Wired into execute-one.ts immediately before the mailbox/legacy branch: on block it calls markFailed(row.id, 'NO_SENDING_MAILBOX', reason), so the row goes to FAILED with a diagnosable error instead of falling through to the mock and being recorded as SENT.
irreversible_actions.evidence: CLOSED 2026-08-09 on branch fix/refuse-mock-send-for-prospect-rows. src/server/email/outbound/prospect-send-transport-guard.test.ts - 8 tests. Fail-closed cases: blocks a prospect row with no mailbox; blocks for EVERY value of EMAIL_PROVIDER including unset, mock and resend (the guard never consults it, so setting the flag cannot reopen the hole); blocks on an empty-string mailbox id, not only null. Non-regression cases: allows a prospect row that HAS a mailbox; allows legacy/platform mail, which carries no contactId, so the pluggable provider stack is untouched. Verified by running the full gate on 2026-08-09: lint exit 0, typecheck exit 0, 1836 tests passed across 214 files (baseline on this branch was 1828/213 - no regressions).
irreversible_actions.known_limitation: The pure decision function is tested; the four-line wiring in execute-one.ts is not covered by an automated test, because executeOutboundSend needs a database and the unit suite is deliberately DB-free. The wiring was verified by reading it. An integration test belongs in execute-one.integration.test.ts when a database is available.
irreversible_actions.design_note: Deliberately NOT behind a feature flag, against the local convention that send-path changes ship flag-off. Justification: this guard can only ever intercept a row that was about to be handed to the legacy ESP stack, which in production is the mock and delivers nothing. It therefore cannot turn a real send into a non-send - it converts a silent fake success into a visible failure. A flag defaulting to off would leave the defect live.

irreversible_actions.action: Send to a recipient on the do-not-contact list belonging to a related domain (bt.com listed, bteurope.com emailed)
irreversible_actions.gate: src/server/outreach/suppression-guard.ts — evaluateSuppression resolves the recipient domain and its parents, then looks them up in SuppressedDomainFamily for THIS client. If the recipient is a listed member of a family and ANY member of that family is on the client do-not-contact list, the send is refused with reason "domain_family". Runs on the SEND path, so a family entry added today protects a contact loaded months ago. Membership is a listed fact recorded by a human via addDomainToFamilyAction; nothing is inferred from the text of a domain.
irreversible_actions.evidence: VERIFIED OPEN. suppression-guard.ts matches domains on an exact unique-key lookup, so a DNC entry for one corporate domain does not cover its sibling domains. The client raised this directly and it is a live compliance exposure, not a theoretical one. Scheduled as Phase 2 (eTLD+1 normalisation via the Public Suffix List, auto-block on strong signals such as a shared Entra tenant id, suggest-only on weak brand-token matches). Exact-match suppression itself works correctly and is tested.
irreversible_actions.what_would_close_it: Phase 2, estimated 6 naive / 18 Tier P days. Sequenced deliberately ahead of the domain-verification work.
irreversible_actions.fail_closed_test_evidence: src/server/outreach/suppression-guard.family.test.ts — 10 tests, SEEN RED FIRST: the three family-blocking cases failed against the unimplemented gate while all seven over-block and per-client-isolation guards already passed, which is the right shape (the danger was never that it under-listed, it was that it would over-block or leak across clients). Green after implementation. Covers: bt.com suppressed blocks bteurope.com; any other family member; subdomains of a member; a family with NO suppressed member blocks nothing; a lookalike is not a member; another client is unaffected; another client suppressing the same domain does NOT inherit this client family; and empty families leave the plain domain rules byte-identical.
irreversible_actions.suppression_behaviour_stated: BOTH, deliberately, and the screen says which. (1) The SEND-PATH gate is authoritative and re-reads families on every send — that is what makes a family entry added today protect a contact loaded last month, the case that actually happens since clients hand over updated sheets weekly. (2) Adding or removing a member ALSO refreshes Contact.isSuppressed for the client, so the lists and counts on screen agree with what the gate will do. Doing only (1) would show a contact as sendable while the gate silently refused it; doing only (2) would leave already-loaded contacts unprotected until someone re-ran a refresh. The UI additionally distinguishes a family that is BLOCKING from one that is LISTED BUT NOT BLOCKING, because a family whose members are none of them suppressed stops nothing and implying otherwise would be the worst outcome of all.
irreversible_actions.ruling: RULING 3, Greg, 2026-08-24: asked whether a client saying "do not contact BT" with bt.com should stop a send to someone at bteurope.com — "do not email them." Covered only via an explicit per-client list, never inferred.

irreversible_actions.action: Ramp a brand-new mailbox straight to full volume instead of warming it up over 30 days
irreversible_actions.gate: src/lib/mailboxes/mailbox-warmup.ts — effectiveDailyCap(mailbox, sendingDays) caps cold-outreach volume from a base of 5/day, stepping +5 every 5 SENDING DAYS up to the mailbox's configured cap. sendingDays is resolved by countSendingDaysForPool (src/server/mailbox/mailbox-sending-history.ts) as DISTINCT UTC dates on which that mailbox actually sent, so a mailbox that has never sent starts at the bottom regardless of how long ago it was connected. Applied at both dispatch planners (send-introduction.ts, controlled-pilot-send.ts) before the reservation transaction opens.
irreversible_actions.evidence: CLOSED - and it was already closed before this session; the earlier record was stale. Verified live on 2026-08-09 against production: `az webapp config appsettings list --name app-opensdoors-outreach-prod --resource-group rg-opensdoors-outreach-prod --query "[?name=='MAILBOX_WARMUP_RAMP']"` returns value 'on', which is the exact string isWarmupRampEnabled() requires. The August roadmap and the engagement notes both recorded this flag as OFF; that is no longer true and those documents should not be trusted on this point. Fail-closed proof in src/lib/mailboxes/mailbox-warmup.test.ts: warmupDailyCap(30, -3) === 5 (clock skew is treated as day 0, the MOST restrictive value, not the least) and warmupDailyCap(30, NaN) === 5 (unknown age also collapses to the base cap); 'never exceeds the mailbox's configured steady cap' asserts the ceiling holds at 30, 20 and custom caps. An unknown or nonsensical input yields the lowest permitted volume, which is what fail-closed means for a ceiling.
irreversible_actions.caveat: The ramp is activated by a flag that DEFAULTS TO OFF, so the gate is fail-closed in its logic but fail-open in its activation: turning MAILBOX_WARMUP_RAMP off silently returns every mailbox to its full configured cap on day one. The unconditional flat per-mailbox cap (30/day) still applies in that case and is separately tested, so the exposure is a missing graduated protection rather than unlimited sending. Re-verify this flag before relying on this entry.
irreversible_actions.gate_defect_2026_08_24: THE GATE IS PRESENT BUT MEASURES THE WRONG THING, so for the mailboxes that matter it does not fire. It ramps on mailbox AGE (connectedAt), not on sends actually made -- its own docstring concedes any mailbox older than the ramp window is unaffected. A mailbox connected months ago during onboarding and never used therefore receives its FULL daily allowance on its first send. Google conditions the rule on a history of SENDING, not an account age. fail_closed_test is being re-earned against the corrected anchor; the files above are the gate and its proof.
irreversible_actions.fail_closed_test_withdrawn_2026_08_24: WITHDRAWN, and this makes the gate report WORSE rather than better, which is the point. The register claimed this gate fails closed. It does not, for the mailboxes that matter. Its test proves the ramp SHAPE (5, +5 every 5 steps) and never asserted that a long-connected, never-used mailbox starts at the bottom -- which is the real-world case, since mailboxes are connected during onboarding and launched weeks later. Anchored on connectedAt, such a mailbox gets its full daily allowance on its first send and the gate is silently inert. A claim of fail-closed that has not been earned is exactly the false-9 this standard exists to stop, so it is withdrawn until the corrected anchor is proven by a test seen RED first.
irreversible_actions.fail_closed_test_evidence: src/lib/mailboxes/mailbox-warmup-history.test.ts — 6 tests, SEEN RED FIRST: 4 of 6 failed against the age anchor, including the case that exposed it ("connected long ago, never sent — still starts at the bottom"). Green after re-anchoring. src/lib/mailboxes/mailbox-warmup.test.ts was also corrected: its previous assertion that a 60-day-old mailbox returns its full cap ENCODED the defect, and now asserts the opposite for a mailbox with zero sending days. Full suite 1881 passing across 217 files.

irreversible_actions.action: Send an outreach email composed for one client to a recipient belonging to a DIFFERENT client's workspace — Client A's campaign drawing Client B's prospect
irreversible_actions.why_irreversible: The mail leaves through a real corporate mailbox and cannot be recalled. It tells Client B's prospect that Client A is contacting them, discloses that OpensDoors holds them as a lead for a second business, and does it under a From: address that is not the one that owns the relationship. It is simultaneously a data-protection breach for the prospect, a confidentiality breach between two paying clients, and a deliverability event on a domain that belongs to neither of them. BC-01 names this as the incident that would end an engagement.
irreversible_actions.recorded_because: It was not in this register at all. BC-01 was rewritten on 2026-08-23 from staff ACCESS isolation (deliberately absent) to workspace DATA isolation (must hold), and this is the irreversible action that rule exists to prevent. Registering it is what makes the rule enforceable rather than aspirational.
irreversible_actions.gate_status: BEING BUILT 2026-08-23. The guards already exist in code; what does NOT yet exist is proof they fail closed, and an end-to-end test of the workspace data boundary. fail_closed_test stays FALSE until that proof is produced and seen RED first. It must not be set to clear a block.
irreversible_actions.gate_files_note: These five ARE the gate and its proof: the policy module holds the four tenant guards (sequence / enrolment / contact / template clientId must equal the send's clientId, src/lib/email-sequences/sequence-send-policy.ts lines 151-177); its unit test proves each guard blocks; the e2e spec proves the boundary end-to-end through the real app; and the seed/fixtures supply the second workspace without which none of it can be exercised.
existing_defences_verified_2026_08_23: Loader scoping: send-introduction.ts loads sequence, step and template scoped by clientId at every hop, and rejects with WRONG_CLIENT if sequence.clientId or template.clientId differs (lines 384, 408).

Policy guards: sequence-send-policy.ts returns blocked_wrong_client when the sequence, enrolment, contact or template belongs to another client — deliberate defence-in-depth, described in its own comment as a second layer 'so a bug in the loader cannot fan out cross-client rows'.
Reply attribution: process-synced-replies.ts matches on clientId + mailboxIdentityId at every leg, and creates NO InboundReply at all when no outbound in that client matches.
Per-client metrics: every count in outreach-metrics.ts carries clientId. Verified live — Client A's activity page shows its prospect and subject, Client B's shows neither.
Suppression: keyed @@unique([clientId, email]) and looked up with clientId, so it is per-workspace by construction.
irreversible_actions.known_hole_2026_08_23: The same mailbox address MAY be connected to two workspaces (@@unique([clientId, emailNormalized]) is per client). Each workspace then stores its own copy of every raw inbound message, including full bodyText, in InboundMailboxMessage. Replies do not cross — no InboundReply is created without a matching outbound in that client — but the raw message store does. Recorded as E-06 in specs/BC-01-tenant-isolation.md.

compensating_controls.for: Absent bounce measurement on the live mailbox send path
compensating_controls.finding: There are no provider delivery webhooks for Graph/Gmail sends, but bounce detection is NOT absent: src/server/mailbox/bounce-detection.ts parses NDR/DSN bounce-backs out of the connected mailbox during inbox sync and is wired into mailbox-inbox-sync.ts. It is gated by MAILBOX_BOUNCE_DETECTION_ENABLED, which DEFAULTS OFF and is absent from .env.example. A reported 0% bounce rate across ~1,209 sends is therefore much more likely to mean 'nothing is measuring' than 'delivery is clean'.
compensating_controls.control: Cap pilot volume hard while the bounce rate is unmeasured, and route the pilot through the controlled-pilot path (src/app/(app)/clients/controlled-pilot-send-actions.ts). Proposed cap: 20 sends per client per day, and no more than 10 per mailbox per day, for the first 10 working days.
compensating_controls.why_that_number: The domain brief's non-negotiable is a bounce rate below 2%. At 20 sends/day a single hard bounce is 5% of the day's volume and 0.5% of a 10-day pilot, so ONE bad address is visible by eye in the reply inbox without any measurement infrastructure at all — that is the point of the number. It also sits inside the product's own warm-up ramp (WARMUP_BASE_CAP 5, +5 every 5 days), so it does not fight the existing control, and inside the researched week-1 guidance of 5-10/day/mailbox.
compensating_controls.trigger_that_lifts_it: BOTH: (1) MAILBOX_BOUNCE_DETECTION_ENABLED=true in Azure App Service config, confirmed by observing at least one real NDR being detected and suppressed; and (2) a measured bounce rate below 2% over a minimum of 200 sends. Until both hold, volume is the substitute for measurement.
compensating_controls.cheaper_first_step: Turn MAILBOX_BOUNCE_DETECTION_ENABLED on. It is an env var on an already-built, already-tested path, not a webhook project.

diagnoses.question: Why does the bounce rate read 0% across 1,209 sends when MAILBOX_BOUNCE_DETECTION_ENABLED is true in production?
diagnoses.answer: DETERMINED, from the code, 2026-08-23. Detection is not broken. The bounce is detected and the address IS suppressed — but the row the report counts is never marked, so the number can only ever read zero.
the_trace: 1. NDRs arrive: mailbox-inbox-sync.ts pulls the connected mailbox and calls processSyncedMessageForBounce BEFORE the internal-mail filter, deliberately, because an NDR usually comes from the tenant's own postmaster.

2. The parser matches: classifyInboundBounce recognises the DSN, extracts the failed recipient, and bounce-detection.ts then requires a matching OutboundEmail (same client, same mailbox, that recipient, actually sent) as a safety gate against spoofed bounces.

3. The result IS written — but only to suppression. suppressRecipientForHardBounce creates the SuppressedEmail row, flips Contact.isSuppressed, and writes one AuditLog row. It receives outboundEmailId and uses it ONLY as audit metadata (bounce-suppression.ts:162).
4. NOTHING EVER SETS OutboundEmail.status = BOUNCED. Neither bounce-detection.ts nor bounce-suppression.ts calls outboundEmail.update at all.
5. The report counts prisma.outboundEmail.count({ clientId, status: 'BOUNCED', ... }). It finds none. It reports 0%.
diagnoses.the_asymmetry: The LEGACY ESP webhook path does mark the row — outbound-provider-events.ts:214-218 sets status 'BOUNCED' and bouncedAt. That is the path the metric was built against. Production does not use it: every real send goes through a connected client mailbox, so every real bounce goes down the NDR path, which suppresses but does not mark. Protection and measurement were wired to two different tables, and only protection got connected to the live transport.
diagnoses.why_this_matters_more_than_it_looks: The reassuring reading — '0% means nothing is measuring, so we are blind' — is wrong in a way that flatters the system. Suppression HAS been working the whole time: bounced addresses have been blocked from future sends. What has been missing is the ability to SEE it. So the deliverability protection is in better shape than feared, and the reporting is in worse shape than feared: it has been silently reporting a clean sheet while bounces were being handled.
diagnoses.how_greg_can_confirm_this_in_one_query: On the production database: SELECT count(*) FROM "SuppressedEmail" WHERE "sourceId" IS NULL; and check AuditLog for rows whose metadata carries providerEventType 'mailbox_sync_ndr'. If those counts are non-zero while OutboundEmail has no BOUNCED rows, the diagnosis is confirmed outright. If BOTH are zero, then NDRs are genuinely not arriving or not parsing, and the trace above is wrong at step 1 or 2.
diagnoses.the_fix_and_its_shape: In processSyncedMessageForBounce, transition the matched OutboundEmail to BOUNCED with bouncedAt = the NDR receipt time, mirroring what the webhook path already does. Small, but it changes send-path behaviour and must land in its own PR with a test seen RED first: assert that an NDR for a real send both suppresses the address AND marks the row, and that a spoofed NDR naming an address this mailbox never wrote to does neither.
diagnoses.not_determined: Whether any NDRs have actually arrived in production. That needs the production database and was not attempted. The code-level defect above is certain; the volume behind it is not.

diagnoses.question: Does the ramp fix change what any currently-connected mailbox may send today?
diagnoses.answer: CANNOT BE ANSWERED FROM THE REPOSITORY — it depends entirely on production data, which was not queried. What IS certain is the shape of the change, and the query that produces the number.
diagnoses.what_changes: Before: cap = f(days since connectedAt). After: cap = f(distinct UTC dates this mailbox actually sent on). For a mailbox that has been sending steadily the two agree and nothing changes. The caps DROP only where a mailbox is older than the ramp window but has little or no sending history — which is precisely the case the fix exists for, and precisely the case being created by onboarding a client ahead of launch.
diagnoses.predicted: OpensDoors' own mailboxes have ~1,209 sends behind them. If those span 25 or more distinct days they are already at the full configured cap and NOTHING changes for them. Bidlow's newly connected mailboxes have zero sending days and will correctly start at 5/day and ramp — which under the old anchor they would ALSO have done, since they are new. The mailboxes that change are any connected weeks ago and not yet launched: they drop from their full cap to 5/day. That is the intended correction, not a regression.
diagnoses.run_this_before_launch: SELECT m.id, m.email, m."dailySendCap", COUNT(DISTINCT DATE(o."sentAt" AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')) AS sending_days, DATE_PART('day', now() - COALESCE(m."connectedAt", m."createdAt")) AS age_days FROM "ClientMailboxIdentity" m LEFT JOIN "OutboundEmail" o ON o."mailboxIdentityId" = m.id AND o."sentAt" IS NOT NULL WHERE m."isActive" GROUP BY m.id, m.email, m."dailySendCap", m."connectedAt", m."createdAt" ORDER BY sending_days ASC;
diagnoses.how_to_read_it: For each row the NEW cap is min(dailySendCap, 5 + 5*floor(sending_days/5)) and the OLD cap was min(dailySendCap, 5 + 5*floor(age_days/5)). Any row where sending_days is far below age_days is a mailbox that was being allowed to send at full volume with no history behind it. That difference is the answer to Greg's question, and it is a number only production can produce.

rulings.ruling: Duplicates are PER CLIENT. A prospect already on THIS client's list is a duplicate and is skipped on import. The same person on a DIFFERENT client's list is NOT a duplicate and is left alone.
rulings.reasoning: Two clients having a relationship with the same person is normal in outreach. Silently blocking one import because another client got there first would be invisible to both of them.
rulings.where_it_lands: DATAMODEL when stage 4 runs. Until then it is recorded here so the CSV import work cannot be scoped against a guess.
rulings.implementation_note: Contact already carries @@unique([clientId, email]), so the per-client uniqueness constraint exists at the database level today. ContactUniverse is deliberately cross-client and deduplicated globally — that is the warehouse, NOT the client list, and Ruling 1 does not change it.
